speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. I understand you are concerned about an 8-month-old boy presenting with feeding difficulties and abdominal distension. To begin our assessment, can you describe the nature of his stools and whether there is any visible blood or mucus present?

speaker: Patient
text: The baby has been very fussy, feeding less than usual, and the abdomen looks distended. Crying gets worse when the belly is touched.

speaker: Doctor
text: The fussiness and tenderness on palpation are concerning signs of abdominal pain. I need to check for signs of obstruction or inflammation, so has the baby had any vomiting, and if so, what color was the vomit?

speaker: Patient
text: There has not been fever, vomiting, or diarrhea like a stomach infection. The baby was born at 39 weeks without birth complications.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that clarification. Since there is no vomiting or fever, I need to assess for constipation, so has the baby passed any stool in the last 24 hours, and if so, what was its consistency?

speaker: Patient
text: The baby did not seem to pass stool normally and the belly swelling has become more obvious. Feeding has clearly decreased over the past few days.

speaker: Doctor
text: The combination of abdominal distension, feeding difficulties, and failure to pass stool normally is highly suggestive of an obstruction. To help differentiate between Hirschsprung disease and other causes, did the baby pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life?

speaker: Patient
text: The abdomen still looks swollen and the baby seems uncomfortable, especially in the lower abdomen.

speaker: Doctor
text: The persistent distension and discomfort without resolution suggest a significant underlying issue that requires immediate visualization. REQUEST TEST: Abdominal_X-Ray
